pos: v. (appointed beforehand; of Christ, appointed before the world was)
etymology: From fore- + ordain, Latin ordinare, to set in order. Peter's Greek is proginosko in its full covenantal sense — foreknown, which in Hebraic usage means chosen and set apart beforehand, not merely observed in advance.
biblical_def: Peter grounds the redemption of sinners in an appointment older than the creation: “Who verily was foreordained before the foundation of the world, but was manifest in these last times for you” (1 Peter 1:20). The Lamb was not an answer improvised after the fall; He was appointed before there was a world to fall. The verse before names the price: “But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot” (1 Peter 1:19). The same epistle opens by putting the church in the same decree: “Elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, through sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ: Grace unto you, and peace, be multiplied” (1 Peter 1:2). Paul locates the choosing at the identical point on the calendar and gives its end: “According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love” (Ephesians 1:4). Note in him. Election is never a bare selection of individuals; it is a choosing of a people in a Head who was Himself foreordained. The decree and the cross are one plan, and neither is a contingency.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines foreordain as to ordain or appoint beforehand; to predetermine.
webster_full: FOREORDAIN, v.t. To ordain or appoint beforehand; to predetermine; to predestinate.
FOREORDINATION, n. Previous ordination or appointment; predetermination; predestination.
ORDAIN, v.t. [L. ordino, from ordo, order.] To set; to establish; to institute; to constitute; to appoint.
DECREE, n. In theology, predetermined purpose of God; the purpose or determination of an immutable Being.
ELECT, v.t. [L. electus, from eligo, to choose.] In theology, to designate, choose or select as an object of mercy or favor.
scriptures: 1 Peter 1:20
Who verily was foreordained before the foundation of the world, but was manifest in these last times for you,
1 Peter 1:19
But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot:
1 Peter 1:2
Elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, through sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ: Grace unto you, and peace, be multiplied.
Ephesians 1:4
According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:
corruption_summary: Foreordination is reduced to foresight — God looking down the corridor of time to see who would choose Him — which makes the decree a report rather than a determination.
corruption_paragraphs: The prescient view holds that God foreknew who would believe and elected them on that basis. It cannot be got out of 1 Peter 1:20, where the object of the same verb is Christ Himself. No one supposes the Father looked ahead, observed that the Son would volunteer, and ratified it. The word means appointed beforehand, and it means the same thing of the Lamb and of the people the Lamb was appointed to redeem. Foreknowledge in Hebraic usage is covenantal knowing — you only have I known of all the families of the earth — not advance information.

Ephesians 1:4 closes the other escape. The choosing is before the foundation of the world, which is before any creature exists to be foreseen doing anything; and its purpose is that we should be holy, which makes holiness the fruit of election rather than its cause. Conditional election reverses both the timing and the direction. The 1689 confesses that God ordained whatsoever comes to pass, yet so that neither is God the author of sin nor is violence offered to the will of the creature — a doctrine that grants the mystery and refuses to resolve it by shrinking the decree.
roots_summary: Greek proginosko (G4267), to know beforehand, foreordain; prognosis (G4268), foreknowledge; eklegomai (G1586), to choose out; proorizo (G4309), to predestinate.
roots_lines: Greek proginosko (G4267) — to foreknow, foreordain; 1 Peter 1:20, of Christ Himself.
Greek prognosis (G4268) — foreknowledge; 1 Peter 1:2 and Acts 2:23, the determinate counsel.
Greek proorizo (G4309) — to mark out beforehand; Romans 8:29 and Ephesians 1:5.
Greek eklegomai (G1586) — to choose out for oneself; Ephesians 1:4, chosen in him.
Hebrew yada (H3045) — to know; Amos 3:2, covenantal knowing, not information.
usage: “Foreordained before the foundation of the world” — and the object is Christ.
“Manifest in these last times for you” — the decree kept its appointment.
“Chosen us in him” — never a bare selection; always in a Head.

pos: n. (the firstborn; a title of rank and right, not of origin)
etymology: From first + begotten. The Greek prototokos renders Hebrew bekor, the firstborn son, who held the double portion and the headship of the house. In Scripture the word is a title of privilege, and it is repeatedly given to sons who were not born first.
biblical_def: Hebrews cites the Father's command concerning His Son: “And again, when he bringeth in the firstbegotten into the world, he saith, And let all the angels of God worship him” (Hebrews 1:6). A creature is never to be worshipped; the command settles the Son's deity in the same breath as His title. John applies the word to the resurrection: “And from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness, and the first begotten of the dead, and the prince of the kings of the earth. Unto him that loved us, and washed us from our sins in his own blood” (Revelation 1:5) — firstbegotten of the dead, the first out of the grave never to return to it, and therefore the guarantee of every believer's rising. Paul states the sense exactly and supplies the purpose clause that defines the term: “And he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence” (Colossians 1:18). Preeminence is what firstborn means. And the Old Testament had already used the title for rank rather than chronology: “Also I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth” (Psalm 89:27) — said of David, who was the eighth son of Jesse.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines firstbegotten as first brought forth; first in the order of nativity; eldest — and notes the use as a title of dignity.
webster_full: FIRSTBEGOTTEN, a. First brought forth; first in the order of nativity; eldest.
FIRSTBORN, a. First brought forth; first in the order of birth; eldest; as the firstborn son.
FIRSTBORN, n. In Scripture, that which is chief, or most excellent; hence, a title of dignity and preeminence.
PREEMINENCE, n. Superiority in excellence; distinction in something commendable; precedence.
BIRTHRIGHT, n. Any right or privilege to which a person is entitled by birth, such as an estate descendible by law to an heir.
scriptures: Hebrews 1:6
And again, when he bringeth in the firstbegotten into the world, he saith, And let all the angels of God worship him.
Revelation 1:5
And from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness, and the first begotten of the dead, and the prince of the kings of the earth. Unto him that loved us, and washed us from our sins in his own blood,
Colossians 1:18
And he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence.
Psalm 89:27
Also I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth.
corruption_summary: Firstborn is read as a statement about origin, and made the basis of the Arian claim that the Son is the first and highest of created things.
corruption_paragraphs: The Arian argument is ancient and it is still made door to door: if Christ is the firstborn of every creature, He is a creature, the first one God made. The word will not bear it. Psalm 89:27 makes David firstborn, and David was the youngest of eight; Ephraim is called firstborn over Manasseh, who was older; Israel is God's firstborn among the nations. Prototokos names rank and right of inheritance, not sequence of manufacture. Colossians 1:18 supplies the definition in its own purpose clause — that in all things he might have the preeminence — and verse 16 has already said that by Him all things were created, which excludes Him from the list.

Hebrews 1:6 is decisive in a different way. The Father commands the angels of God to worship the firstbegotten. Scripture forbids the worship of any creature with unusual severity; John is twice rebuked by an angel for attempting it. A command from the Father that all angels worship this One is a declaration of full deity, and the Nicene confession that He is begotten, not made, being of one substance with the Father, is precisely the doctrine of this verse. Begotten in the eternal generation of the Son is not an event; it is an eternal relation within the one undivided Godhead.
roots_summary: Greek prototokos (G4416), firstborn; arche (G746), beginning, first rank; proteuo (G4409), to have preeminence; Hebrew bekor (H1060), firstborn.
roots_lines: Greek prototokos (G4416) — firstborn; of rank and inheritance, Colossians 1:15, 18 and Hebrews 1:6.
Greek proteuo (G4409) — to hold the first place; Colossians 1:18, the purpose clause that defines the title.
Greek monogenes (G3439) — only begotten; the distinct term of John 1:14, 18 and 3:16.
Hebrew bekor (H1060) — firstborn; the double portion of Deuteronomy 21:17.
Hebrew bekorah (H1062) — birthright; what Esau sold for one meal, Genesis 25:33.
usage: “Let all the angels of God worship him” — a command no creature could receive.
“The first begotten of the dead” — the first out never to return.
“I will make him my firstborn” — said of Jesse's eighth son.

pos: n. (one who runs ahead to prepare the way; a title of Christ within the veil)
etymology: From fore- + runner. The Greek prodromos was used of the scout who ran ahead of an army and of the small boat that carried a ship's cable into harbour ahead of the vessel. Hebrews uses it of Christ entering heaven ahead of His people.
biblical_def: Hebrews gives Christ a title no other person in Scripture receives: “Whither the forerunner is for us entered, even Jesus, made an high priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec” (Hebrews 6:20). The word carries its own argument. A forerunner goes first, and he goes first on behalf of those who follow — for us — which is why the high priest of Israel, who went into the holy of holies alone and came out again, was never called one. The image before it is nautical and deliberate: “Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast, and which entereth into that within the veil” (Hebrews 6:19). The anchor of this ship is not on the seabed but inside the sanctuary, fastened to a Person. And the destination is not a room in Jerusalem: “For Christ is not entered into the holy places made with hands, which are the figures of the true; but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God for us” (Hebrews 9:24). What follows for the believer is the hope of arriving where the anchor already is: “If by any means I might attain unto the resurrection of the dead” (Philippians 3:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a forerunner as a messenger sent before to give notice of the approach of others; a harbinger; a precursor; and, that which precedes and announces.
webster_full: FORERUNNER, n. A messenger sent before to give notice of the approach of others; a harbinger.
FORERUNNER, n. A prognostic; a sign foreshowing something to follow; as, a bright rainbow is a forerunner of fair weather.
FORERUN, v.t. To advance before; to come before as an earnest of something to follow.
HARBINGER, n. In former times, an officer of the king's household who went before and provided lodgings; a forerunner; a precursor.
ANCHOR, n. [L. anchora.] An iron instrument for holding a ship at rest in water. In Scripture, that which gives stability and security.
scriptures: Hebrews 6:20
Whither the forerunner is for us entered, even Jesus, made an high priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec.
Hebrews 6:19
Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast, and which entereth into that within the veil;
Hebrews 9:24
For Christ is not entered into the holy places made with hands, which are the figures of the true; but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God for us:
Philippians 3:11
If by any means I might attain unto the resurrection of the dead.
corruption_summary: Christ is offered as an example who blazed a trail others must now walk in their own strength, when the title forerunner means He entered on their behalf and secured their entry.
corruption_paragraphs: The exemplarist reading of the atonement — Christ as pioneer, pattern, moral influence — can quote this verse and miss its two most important words. For us. A forerunner does not merely demonstrate that a harbour can be reached; the prodromos boat carried the cable in so that the ship could be drawn after it. Hebrews is not describing a technique for entering heaven. It is describing a Priest who entered and holds the line, and the anchor in verse 19 is already inside the veil while the ship is still at sea.

The verse also answers Rome's sanctuary. Hebrews 9:24 says Christ entered not into the holy places made with hands but into heaven itself; He appears in the presence of God for us, once, and the offering is not repeated. Every system that keeps a priesthood, an altar, and a re-presented sacrifice on earth has built a figure of the true after the true has come. And the Melchizedek order named in 6:20 is the point: a priesthood without succession, because the Priest does not die.
roots_summary: Greek prodromos (G4274), a forerunner, scout; agkura (G45), an anchor; katapetasma (G2665), the veil; emphanizo (G1718), to appear before.
roots_lines: Greek prodromos (G4274) — one who runs before; only Hebrews 6:20, and of Christ.
Greek agkura (G45) — an anchor; fastened inside the veil, not on the seabed.
Greek katapetasma (G2665) — the veil; rent from top to bottom at the cross, Matthew 27:51.
Greek emphanizo (G1718) — to appear, present oneself; Hebrews 9:24, in the presence of God for us.
Hebrew Malki-Tsedeq (H4442) — Melchizedek, king of righteousness; the order without succession.
usage: “The forerunner is for us entered” — two words carry the whole gospel.
“An anchor of the soul…within the veil” — the anchor is already in port.
“Not…made with hands, but into heaven itself” — the true, not the figure.

pos: adj. (implanted; of the word received into the soul)
etymology: From en- + graft, Greek graphion, a stylus, from the shape of the scion. James's Greek is emphutos, inborn or implanted — a word from horticulture describing something set into a stock so as to live from it.
biblical_def: James makes the reception of the word a matter of soil rather than of study: “Wherefore lay apart all filthiness and superfluity of naughtiness, and receive with meekness the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls” (James 1:21). Two things precede the receiving. Filth is laid aside, and meekness is put on — the teachable lowliness of a man who expects to be corrected. The word is called engrafted because it is not information laid alongside a life but a living scion set into a stock, drawing from the root and bearing the root's fruit. Paul uses the same horticulture of the Gentiles brought into the covenant: “And if some of the branches be broken off, and thou, being a wild olive tree, wert graffed in among them, and with them partakest of the root and fatness of the olive tree” (Romans 11:17), and warns against boasting in it: “For if thou wert cut out of the olive tree which is wild by nature, and wert graffed contrary to nature into a good olive tree: how much more shall these, which be the natural branches, be graffed into their own olive tree?” (Romans 11:24). The Lord Jesus states the principle at its root: “I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing” (John 15:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines engraft as to insert a scion of one tree or plant into another for propagation; and figuratively, to set or fix deep and firm.
webster_full: ENGRAFT, v.t. To insert a scion of one tree or plant into another for propagation; as, to engraft a pear-scion on a quince.
ENGRAFT, v.t. To plant or introduce something foreign into that which is native, for the purpose of propagation.
ENGRAFT, v.t. To set or fix deep and firm; as, engrafted habits or principles.
SCION, n. A shoot or sprout of a plant; a young shoot or twig, suitable for grafting.
MEEKNESS, n. Softness of temper; mildness; gentleness; forbearance under injuries and provocations.
scriptures: James 1:21
Wherefore lay apart all filthiness and superfluity of naughtiness, and receive with meekness the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls.
Romans 11:17
And if some of the branches be broken off, and thou, being a wild olive tree, wert graffed in among them, and with them partakest of the root and fatness of the olive tree;
Romans 11:24

For if thou wert cut out of the olive tree which is wild by nature, and wert graffed contrary to nature into a good olive tree: how much more shall these, which be the natural branches, be graffed into their own olive tree?
John 15:5
I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.
corruption_summary: Scripture is treated as material to be mastered, so that the hearer approaches as a critic or a collector rather than as the stock into which a living word is being set.
corruption_paragraphs: James 1:21 puts two conditions before the reception of the word, and neither is intellectual. Lay apart the filth; receive with meekness. A man may know the languages, the systems, and the history, and be an unfit hearer on both counts. The horticultural figure explains why: a graft does not take in a stock that will not receive it. This is a rebuke to the informational approach to the Bible — verses collected, arguments won, nothing grafted — and James follows it immediately with the man who beholds himself in a glass and forgets what manner of man he was.

Romans 11 keeps the figure honest in the matter of Israel. Paul says the wild branch was graffed contrary to nature, which is a standing rebuke to Gentile presumption, and he expressly warns against boasting against the natural branches. Replacement theology reads the olive tree as though the wild branch had become the root. Paul's argument runs the other way: the root bears thee, thou bearest not the root. And John 15:5 gives the bare terms of every grafted life — without me ye can do nothing.
roots_summary: Greek emphutos (G1721), implanted, engrafted; prautes (G4240), meekness; egkentrizo (G1461), to graft in; meno (G3306), to abide.
roots_lines: Greek emphutos (G1721) — implanted, inborn; only James 1:21, the engrafted word.
Greek egkentrizo (G1461) — to graft in; six times in Romans 11.
Greek prautes (G4240) — meekness; the posture of a stock that will receive a scion.
Greek meno (G3306) — to abide, remain; John 15, the verb of the whole vine discourse.
Greek rhiza (G4491) — a root; Romans 11:18, the root bears thee.
usage: “Receive with meekness the engrafted word” — a scion, not a file.
“Graffed contrary to nature” — the Gentile has nothing to boast of.
“Without me ye can do nothing” — the terms of every grafted life.

pos: adj. (made of one form with; of Paul, shaped to the death of Christ)
etymology: From Latin conformare, to shape together, from forma, a form. Paul's Greek is summorphizomenos, from morphe, the form that expresses the essence — not a resemblance put on but a shape worked in.
biblical_def: Paul states the whole aim of his life in one sentence with three clauses, and the order is not the one a reader expects: “That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, being made conformable unto his death” (Philippians 3:10). Knowing, then resurrection power, then the fellowship of sufferings, then conformity to His death. Paul is not asking for an easier life on the strength of the resurrection; he asks to be shaped into the likeness of a crucifixion. The hope that follows is the reason such a request is not morbid: “If by any means I might attain unto the resurrection of the dead” (Philippians 3:11). The same conforming is the settled purpose of God for every elect soul: “For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren” (Romans 8:29). The end of election is not bare rescue but resemblance. And the manner of the work is progressive and by the Spirit: “But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Corinthians 3:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines conformable as corresponding in form, or in essential character; suitable; agreeable; and, of persons, compliant.
webster_full: CONFORMABLE, a. Corresponding in form, or in the external shape; having the same or similar external appearance.
CONFORMABLE, a. Suitable; consistent; agreeable; as, nature is conformable to herself.
CONFORM, v.t. [L. conformo; con and forma, form.] To make like in external appearance; to reduce to a like shape or form with something else.
CONFORMITY, n. Likeness; correspondence with a model or pattern; resemblance; agreement.
TRANSFORM, v.t. To change the form of; to change the shape or appearance; to metamorphose.
scriptures: Philippians 3:10
That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, being made conformable unto his death;
Philippians 3:11
If by any means I might attain unto the resurrection of the dead.
Romans 8:29
For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren.
2 Corinthians 3:18
But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord.
corruption_summary: Conformity to Christ is recast as a programme of self-improvement or as a technique for accessing resurrection power, with the death Paul asks to be shaped into quietly omitted.
corruption_paragraphs: Philippians 3:10 is often quoted as far as the power of his resurrection and stopped there. The sentence does not stop; it runs on to the fellowship of His sufferings and to being made conformable unto His death, and Paul's grammar binds the four together as one petition. A spirituality that wants the power without the conformity has asked for half of a request that Scripture makes indivisible. The apostle is writing from custody, and he had already counted his pedigree loss for this.

The other corruption makes the whole thing a self-improvement project. Romans 8:29 forbids it: the conforming is what God predestinated, worked by Him toward an end that is His own glory — that His Son might be the firstborn among many brethren. And 2 Corinthians 3:18 gives the means, which is beholding rather than striving: we are changed, passively, as we look. Sanctification is real effort and it is not self-manufacture. The 1689 has it exactly: the saints grow in grace by the continual supply of strength from Christ, not by a strength of their own.
roots_summary: Greek summorphizo (G4833), to make of like form; summorphos (G4832), conformed; morphe (G3444), essential form; metamorphoo (G3339), to transform.
roots_lines: Greek summorphizo (G4833) — to be conformed to; Philippians 3:10, unto his death.
Greek summorphos (G4832) — conformed, of like form; Romans 8:29, to the image of his Son.
Greek morphe (G3444) — the form expressing the essence; Philippians 2:6, the form of God.
Greek metamorphoo (G3339) — to be transformed; 2 Corinthians 3:18 and Romans 12:2.
Greek koinonia (G2842) — fellowship, sharing; the fellowship of his sufferings.
usage: “Being made conformable unto his death” — the clause usually left off.
“Predestinate to be conformed” — the end of election is resemblance.
“Changed…from glory to glory” — passive, and by beholding.

pos: n. (an ointment for the eyes; what Christ tells Laodicea to buy of Him)
etymology: From eye + salve, Old English sealf, an ointment. The Greek kollourion was a Phrygian eye-preparation, and Laodicea was known for it — Christ offers the city's own famous remedy for a blindness the city did not know it had.
biblical_def: The last of the seven letters is written to a church whose self-assessment is the problem: “Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked” (Revelation 3:17). Every word of their account of themselves is contradicted, and the last two items — blind and naked — name what they cannot see about themselves. Christ's answer is commerce: “I counsel thee to buy of me gold tried in the fire, that thou mayest be rich; and white raiment, that thou mayest be clothed, and that the shame of thy nakedness do not appear; and anoint thine eyes with eyesalve, that thou mayest see” (Revelation 3:18). The three purchases answer the three lacks exactly, and the price is stated elsewhere in Isaiah's terms — without money and without price. Then the tone, which is the surprise of the letter: “As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten: be zealous therefore, and repent” (Revelation 3:19). The severest of the seven letters is addressed to a church He loves. Paul prays for the same faculty: “The eyes of your understanding being enlightened; that ye may know what is the hope of his calling, and what the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints” (Ephesians 1:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines eye-salve as ointment for the eye; and salve as a glutinous composition or substance to be applied to wounds or sores.
webster_full: EYE-SALVE, n. Ointment for the eye.
SALVE, n. [Sax. sealf.] A glutinous composition or substance to be applied to wounds or sores; when spread on leather or cloth, it is called a plaster.
SALVE, v.t. To heal by applications or medicaments; to help; to remedy.
ANOINT, v.t. To pour oil upon; to smear or rub over with oil or unctuous substances.
LUKEWARM, a. Moderately warm; tepid. Figuratively, indifferent; not ardent; not zealous.
scriptures: Revelation 3:17
Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked:
Revelation 3:18

I counsel thee to buy of me gold tried in the fire, that thou mayest be rich; and white raiment, that thou mayest be clothed, and that the shame of thy nakedness do not appear; and anoint thine eyes with eyesalve, that thou mayest see.
Revelation 3:19
As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten: be zealous therefore, and repent.
Ephesians 1:18
The eyes of your understanding being enlightened; that ye may know what is the hope of his calling, and what the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints,
corruption_summary: Laodicea is read as a warning to churches other than one's own, which is the precise failure the letter describes — a congregation confident of its own diagnosis.
corruption_paragraphs: The letter is quoted constantly, and almost always about somebody else: the liberal denomination, the prosperity church, the congregation across town. Laodicea's condition was not that it held false doctrine — nothing in the letter says so — but that its self-assessment was wrong and it did not know. Thou sayest…and knowest not. A church certain it is not Laodicea has produced the only symptom the letter lists. The eyesalve is prescribed for exactly that blindness, and it must be bought of Christ, which means the remedy is not more self-examination but His verdict received.

Verse 19 is the part most often omitted, and it changes the letter. As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten. The harshest words in the seven letters are spoken by One who names the rebuke as evidence of love, and the next verse has Him standing at the door and knocking — a picture usually preached to unbelievers and addressed in its context to a church. Hebrews 12 teaches the same: the son whom the Father receiveth, He scourgeth. A congregation that never hears a hard word about itself should not conclude it is loved.
roots_summary: Greek kollourion (G2854), eyesalve; egchrio (G1472), to rub in, anoint; chliaros (G5513), lukewarm; elegcho (G1651), to rebuke, convict.
roots_lines: Greek kollourion (G2854) — an eye-ointment; only Revelation 3:18, and a Laodicean specialty.
Greek egchrio (G1472) — to rub in, anoint; the verb of applying the salve.
Greek chliaros (G5513) — lukewarm; Revelation 3:16, neither cold nor hot.
Greek elegcho (G1651) — to convict, rebuke; verse 19, named as an act of love.
Greek agorazo (G59) — to buy in the market; buy of me, the commerce of grace.
usage: “Thou sayest, I am rich…and knowest not” — the whole disease in one clause.
“Anoint thine eyes with eyesalve” — the city's own famous remedy, offered by Christ.
“As many as I love, I rebuke” — the severest letter, to a church He loves.

pos: n. pl. (citizens together; the standing of Gentiles in the commonwealth of God)
etymology: From fellow + citizen. Paul's Greek is sumpolitai, from polis, a city — sharing one civic register. The word is chosen against the two terms in the same sentence that it abolishes: strangers and foreigners.
biblical_def: Paul first states what the Gentiles were, and holds nothing back: “That at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world” (Ephesians 2:12). Five disqualifications in one verse. Then the hinge: “But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13). And then the new standing, stated in civic and domestic terms together: “Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19). A stranger had no rights; a foreigner was a resident alien with some protection and no standing; a fellowcitizen is on the register. And Paul does not stop at citizenship, which is a legal category, but adds the household, which is a family one — the Gentile is enrolled and adopted. The same register is named again as the Christian's true home: “For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ” (Philippians 3:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a fellow-citizen as one of the same city, state or nation — and a citizen as an inhabitant enjoying the freedom and privileges of the city in which he resides.
webster_full: FELLOW-CITIZEN, n. A citizen of the same state or nation.
CITIZEN, n. The native of a city, or an inhabitant who enjoys the freedom and privileges of the city in which he resides.
ALIEN, a. [L. alienus.] Foreign; not belonging to the same country, land or government; estranged; belonging to another.
STRANGER, n. A foreigner; one who belongs to another country; one not entitled to the privileges of a citizen.
HOUSEHOLD, n. Those who dwell under the same roof and compose a family; a family living together.
scriptures: Ephesians 2:12
That at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world:
Ephesians 2:13
But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ.
Ephesians 2:19
Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God;
Philippians 3:20
For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ:
corruption_summary: Ephesians 2 is pressed into service for a general programme of inclusion, when Paul's argument is about a specific covenant standing conferred by a specific price.
corruption_paragraphs: The chapter is a favourite of the inclusion sermon, and the sermon usually drops verse 13. Paul names the means precisely: those who were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ. Not by welcome, not by the erasure of the categories, but by a death that satisfied the law standing between them. Three verses later he says Christ abolished in His flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances. An inclusion preached without the blood is not this chapter's inclusion, and it cannot deliver what this chapter delivers.

The opposite error underestimates verse 19. Some Christians live as though they were still on probation — tolerated, resident, hoping not to be noticed. Paul uses the two strongest available words against that: fellowcitizens, on the register with the saints, and of the household of God, which is adoption. An adopted son does not have a lesser sonship. The former state in verse 12 was genuinely as bleak as Paul says — no hope, and without God in the world — and the new one is genuinely as full.
roots_summary: Greek sumpolites (G4847), a fellow-citizen; xenos (G3581), a stranger; paroikos (G3941), a resident alien; oikeios (G3609), of the household.
roots_lines: Greek sumpolites (G4847) — fellow-citizen; only Ephesians 2:19.
Greek xenos (G3581) — a stranger, with no standing at all.
Greek paroikos (G3941) — a resident alien, tolerated and not enrolled.
Greek oikeios (G3609) — belonging to the house; the family word Paul adds to the civic one.
Greek politeuma (G4175) — commonwealth, register; Philippians 3:20.
usage: “Having no hope, and without God in the world” — the former estate, stated plainly.
“Made nigh by the blood of Christ” — the means, not the welcome.
“Fellowcitizens…and of the household” — enrolled and adopted.

pos: n. pl. (men who do not keep their word; an item in Paul's indictment of the race)
etymology: From covenant + breaker. Paul's Greek is asunthetos, literally uncovenanted or untrustworthy in an agreement — a man with whom nothing can be settled, because his word does not hold.
biblical_def: Romans 1 ends with a list of what a race given over to itself becomes, and the items are not all spectacular: “Without understanding, covenantbreakers, without natural affection, implacable, unmerciful” (Romans 1:31). Four of the five are failures of ordinary human bonds — the man whose word cannot be relied on, the parent or child without natural love, the person who will not be reconciled, the one who will not show mercy. Paul's catalogue does not treat these as lesser sins than the ones that opened the chapter. And the summary charge is that the doing is not the worst of it: “Who knowing the judgment of God, that they which commit such things are worthy of death, not only do the same, but have pleasure in them that do them” (Romans 1:32). The parallel list in the Pastorals names the same vice under another word: “Without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good” (2 Timothy 3:3). Behind the human failure stands the covenant Israel broke, and the grief of the God who kept His: “Not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day that I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt; which my covenant they brake, although I was an husband unto them, saith the LORD” (Jeremiah 31:32).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a covenant-breaker as one who violates his covenant; and covenant as a mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons, to do or to forbear some act.
webster_full: COVENANT-BREAKER, n. One who violates his covenant.
COVENANT, n. [L. con and venio, to come together.] A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons, to do or to forbear some act or thing; a contract; stipulation.
COVENANT, n. In theology, the covenant of works is that implied in the commands, prohibitions and promises of God; the covenant of redemption is the mutual agreement between the Father and Son.
IMPLACABLE, a. [L. implacabilis.] Not to be appeased; that cannot be pacified or rendered peaceable; inexorable.
TRUCE-BREAKER, n. One who violates a truce, covenant or engagement.
scriptures: Romans 1:31
Without understanding, covenantbreakers, without natural affection, implacable, unmerciful:
Romans 1:32
Who knowing the judgment of God, that they which commit such things are worthy of death, not only do the same, but have pleasure in them that do them.
2 Timothy 3:3
Without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good,
Jeremiah 31:32

Not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day that I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt; which my covenant they brake, although I was an husband unto them, saith the LORD:
corruption_summary: Breaking one's word is reclassified as a matter of changed circumstances or personal growth, and the vice Paul names loses its name.
corruption_paragraphs: Asunthetos describes the man with whom nothing can be finally settled. Modern usage does not have a word for this as a vice; it has a vocabulary of explanation instead. The contract was renegotiated. The marriage had run its course. He needed to be true to himself. Paul puts the failure in a list with implacability and want of natural affection, because they share a root: a self that will not be bound by anything outside itself. Ecclesiastes says defer not to pay a vow, for God hath no pleasure in fools; better it is that thou shouldest not vow than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.

Romans 1:32 names the aggravation, and it is the sentence that reaches respectable people. It is one thing to do such things; it is worse to take pleasure in them that do them. A society that celebrates the broken covenant — that makes entertainment of the abandoned family and applause of the discarded vow — has arrived at the last clause of the chapter. Jeremiah 31:32 is the answer and the comfort: the covenant Israel broke was kept from the other side by One who calls Himself a husband to them, and the new covenant He promises is written not on tables but on hearts.
roots_summary: Greek asunthetos (G802), covenant-breaking, untrustworthy; aspondos (G786), truce-breaking, implacable; astorgos (G794), without natural affection; Hebrew berith (H1285), covenant.
roots_lines: Greek asunthetos (G802) — not keeping an agreement; only Romans 1:31.
Greek aspondos (G786) — admitting no truce; rendered implacable and trucebreakers.
Greek astorgos (G794) — without family affection; in both lists, Romans 1:31 and 2 Timothy 3:3.
Hebrew berith (H1285) — a covenant; the bond God keeps and men break.
Hebrew parar (H6565) — to break, annul; Jeremiah 31:32, my covenant they brake.
usage: “Covenantbreakers…implacable, unmerciful” — failures of ordinary bonds, in the same list.
“Have pleasure in them that do them” — the aggravation that reaches the respectable.
“Although I was an husband unto them” — the covenant kept from the other side.

pos: n. pl. (the burial wrappings; what Lazarus came out in and Christ left behind)
etymology: From grave + clothes. John's Greek is keiriai, the linen strips wound about a corpse. The detail is reported twice in the Gospel, and the difference between the two accounts is the difference between a resuscitation and a resurrection.
biblical_def: Lazarus comes out of the tomb still bound: “And he that was dead came forth, bound hand and foot with graveclothes: and his face was bound about with a napkin. Jesus saith unto them, Loose him, and let him go” (John 11:44). He walks out under his own wrappings and needs other hands to free him, because he has been restored to the life he had and will one day die again. The command that raised him is four words: “And when he thus had spoken, he cried with a loud voice, Lazarus, come forth” (John 11:43). Set beside this the empty tomb of chapter 20: “And the napkin, that was about his head, not lying with the linen clothes, but wrapped together in a place by itself” (John 20:7). No one loosed Him. The cloths are left where the body had been, the head-napkin folded by itself, and the Occupant is gone — a body raised into a different order of life, which grave-wrappings no longer hold. The claim He had made to Martha before either tomb was opened stands over both: “Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live” (John 11:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines grave-clothes as the clothes or dress in which the dead are interred.
webster_full: GRAVE-CLOTHES, n. The clothes or dress in which the dead are interred.
GRAVE, n. [Sax. graef, from grafan, to dig.] A pit or trench in the earth; the place where a dead human body is deposited.
NAPKIN, n. [Fr. nappe, a cloth.] A cloth used for wiping the hands; a handkerchief.
SHROUD, n. The dress of the dead; a winding sheet.
RESURRECTION, n. [L. resurgo, to rise again.] A rising again; chiefly, the revival of the dead of the human race, or their return from the grave.
scriptures: John 11:44
And he that was dead came forth, bound hand and foot with graveclothes: and his face was bound about with a napkin. Jesus saith unto them, Loose him, and let him go.
John 11:43
And when he thus had spoken, he cried with a loud voice, Lazarus, come forth.
John 20:7
And the napkin, that was about his head, not lying with the linen clothes, but wrapped together in a place by itself.
John 11:25
Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live:
corruption_summary: The resurrection of Christ is reduced to a resuscitation like Lazarus's, or to a spiritual survival with no body involved — and John's account of the linen answers both.
corruption_paragraphs: John reports the cloths twice, and the contrast is the argument. Lazarus emerges wrapped and must be untied; he has been given back the life he had. Christ's wrappings are left in the tomb, the napkin folded by itself, and He is not there. The Gospel is telling the reader that these are not the same kind of event. Every theory that makes Easter a resuscitation — a swoon, a revival, a return — has to account for a body that left its own bindings behind and afterward passed through doors and ate broiled fish.

The opposite theory makes the resurrection wholly spiritual, a persistence of influence or of the disciples' faith. John 20:7 is an awkward verse for it, because a purely spiritual resurrection requires no linen at all, and an evangelist inventing one would not stop to mention the placement of a head-cloth. The 1689 confesses the resurrection of the selfsame bodies, and none other, and Christ's empty wrappings are the first instance of what is promised to all His people. Lazarus died again. The One who called him did not.
roots_summary: Greek keiria (G2750), a grave-band, winding strip; soudarion (G4676), a napkin, face-cloth; othonion (G3608), linen cloths; anastasis (G386), resurrection.
roots_lines: Greek keiria (G2750) — a burial band; only John 11:44, rendered graveclothes.
Greek soudarion (G4676) — a face-cloth; on Lazarus's face, and folded by itself in John 20:7.
Greek othonion (G3608) — strips of linen; the wrappings left in the empty tomb.
Greek entulisso (G1794) — to wrap or fold together; the napkin in a place by itself.
Greek anastasis (G386) — a standing up again; John 11:25, I am the resurrection.
usage: “Bound hand and foot with graveclothes” — and other hands had to loose him.
“Wrapped together in a place by itself” — no one loosed Him.
“I am the resurrection, and the life” — said before either tomb was opened.

pos: adj. (weak, easily broken; what David asked to be taught about himself)
etymology: From Latin fragilis, breakable, from frangere, to break. Psalm 39:4 uses it for Hebrew chadel, ceasing or transient — and David asks to be shown it, which makes frailty a lesson rather than merely a condition.
biblical_def: David makes a request that few would make: “LORD, make me to know mine end, and the measure of my days, what it is; that I may know how frail I am” (Psalm 39:4). He is not asking for a date; he is asking to be taught the fact he already knows and does not feel. Frailty is the one universal condition that men successfully forget, and David treats the forgetting as the danger. The figures Scripture gives are agricultural and brief: “As for man, his days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth” (Psalm 103:15), and the prophet is given the same word as his commission: “The voice said, Cry. And he said, What shall I cry? All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field” (Isaiah 40:6). James turns it on the businessman's calendar: “Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away” (James 4:14). None of these passages ends in despair. Isaiah 40 goes straight on to say that the word of our God shall stand for ever, and Psalm 103 follows the grass with the mercy of the LORD from everlasting to everlasting.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines frail as weak; infirm; liable to fail and decay; subject to casualties; easily destroyed; perishable; not firm or durable.
webster_full: FRAIL, a. [L. fragilis, from frango, to break.] Weak; infirm; liable to fail and decay; subject to casualties; easily destroyed; perishable; not firm or durable.
FRAIL, a. Weak in mind or resolution; liable to error or deception.
FRAILTY, n. Weakness of resolution; infirmity; liableness to be deceived or seduced.
FRAILTY, n. Frailness; infirmity of body; instability; liableness to decay and perish.
VAPOR, n. [L. vapor.] In a general sense, an invisible elastic fluid, rendered aeriform by heat; steam; that which is fleeting and unsubstantial.
scriptures: Psalm 39:4
LORD, make me to know mine end, and the measure of my days, what it is; that I may know how frail I am.
Psalm 103:15
As for man, his days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth.
Isaiah 40:6
The voice said, Cry. And he said, What shall I cry? All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field:
James 4:14
Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away.
corruption_summary: Mortality is managed rather than known — postponed by medicine, hidden by the funeral trade, deferred by the calendar — and the instruction David asked for is unavailable.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern arrangement is not that men deny death but that they are never taught it. The dying are moved out of the house, the dead are handled by professionals, and the word itself is replaced. What David asks for in Psalm 39:4 — to be made to know the measure of his days — a whole civilization is organized to prevent. Moses prayed the same: so teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom. Wisdom in Scripture has a prerequisite, and the prerequisite is a true estimate of one's own length.

The opposite error is to make frailty the last word, which Scripture never does. Every passage that calls man grass has a clause after it. Isaiah 40:6 is followed by the word of our God shall stand for ever, which Peter quotes and applies to the gospel preached. Psalm 103 follows the flower of the field with mercy from everlasting to everlasting upon them that fear Him. James 4:14 is followed by the right sentence to say about tomorrow: if the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that. Frailty known drives a man out of himself, which is exactly where it was meant to send him.
roots_summary: Hebrew chadel (H2310), transient, ceasing; chatsir (H2682), grass; tsits (H6731), a flower; Greek atmis (G822), a vapour.
roots_lines: Hebrew chadel (H2310) — frail, fleeting; Psalm 39:4, what David asked to be taught.
Hebrew chatsir (H2682) — grass; Psalm 103:15 and Isaiah 40:6.
Hebrew tsits (H6731) — a blossom; the flower of the field that fades.
Greek atmis (G822) — a vapour, mist; James 4:14, appearing a little time.
Hebrew manah (H4487) — to number, appoint; Psalm 90:12, so teach us to number our days.
usage: “That I may know how frail I am” — a fact asked for as a lesson.
“All flesh is grass” — and the next clause is the word that stands.
“It is even a vapour” — said to men making a two-year plan.
